Implication for the eventual pattern: this is a second real occurrence of a destructive git operation accidentally clobbering another session's (or the same session's own) uncommitted work in the shared tree, following the earlier unresolved silent-revert incident. Unlike that one, this one was caught immediately and explained precisely, because the standing verification floor happened to sit downstream of it. Worth treating as evidence that the "always verify against real source, never trust a report" discipline isn't just about catching a peer's inaccurate claim — it's also the safety net that makes a shared-working-tree design survivable when something (a subagent, a stray command) does go wrong at the git level. Doesn't argue for worktrees on its own, but does argue the routine verification floor should never be treated as optional or skippable "just this once," since its value showed up here in a way nobody was specifically testing for.

summary: [GENERAL] Centralized issue/task management in the coordinator's native tasks, evidence-gated open/close cycle
body:
Ventsislav introduced a significant new coordination layer on top of everything already running: centralized issue/gap management, using the coordinator's own native Claude Code task list (TaskCreate/TaskUpdate/TaskList) as the SINGLE place every open item across the whole fleet lives — not just the tool-build pipeline's own lifecycle tracking (the 8-stage Jira Lifecycle protocol), but every deferred decision, unresolved question, known gap, and follow-up any session surfaces, across BOTH repos (core-tech-mcp and orchestration-layer).

WHY this was needed, concretely, not hypothetically: a full-fleet sweep (every managed session asked to introspect its own context for anything outstanding/undecided/deferred) surfaced roughly 30 genuinely distinct items in one pass — architectural gaps (the v2/service credential wall blocking 9 tools), open design questions (sensitive-content exposure pattern for n8n/security-review output), cross-cutting technical debt (a rate-budget window-expiry test gap flagged independently 3 separate times across different tools' reviews, a duplicated docblock pattern across 10+ files), and even items in the OTHER repo (orchestration-layer's cost-center message-field enumeration-oracle risk, a docstring/behavior mismatch on CostCenterUnavailableError). Before this sweep, each of these existed only in whichever single session's own context window had found it — with no shared place to see the full picture, several were already at risk of being re-discovered independently (the tool-budget window-expiry gap WAS re-discovered three separate times before anyone connected the dots) or lost entirely once that session's context got compacted or the session ended.

MECHANISM, as it actually works now: every managed session (including the PM) periodically sweeps its own context on request and reports every open item, with enough detail to act on, directly to the coordinator. The coordinator mints ONE native task per item (via TaskCreate), in its own session, as the single source of truth. Critically, this is NOT a write-once log: the standing rule requires every session to report back to the coordinator the MOMENT any previously-deferred/undecided/gapped item gets resolved during later work, WITH hard evidence (a commit SHA, a direct quote from the human, a freshly-verified fact) — not a vague "handled." The coordinator then updates or closes (TaskUpdate) that exact native task using that evidence, so the task list stays a live, accurate reflection of true state rather than degrading into a stale wishlist the way the Jira "21 tools tested" over-report or the "COTE-1412 is delete-env-var" ticket-mixup incidents (both logged earlier this session) already showed CAN happen when status claims aren't evidence-gated.

A second, explicit design point: any session holding its OWN native CC tasks (several had accumulated some independently, e.g. Reviwer's earlier 8 cross-cutting cleanup items) must transfer them to the coordinator's list and delete their own copies — there is deliberately no secondary task list anywhere in the fleet. This mirrors the earlier field-note pattern about consolidating field-notes centrally, but applied to actionable work-tracking rather than narrative history.

One friction point surfaced immediately: the PM correctly refused to adopt "centralized tracking is now standing" purely from the coordinator's relayed framing ("confirmed by Ventsislav") — it held the line until it got Ventsislav's own direct confirmation, even though the underlying instruction was accurate. This is the SAME verify-before-acting discipline already logged multiple times this session, now demonstrated specifically protecting a structural/process change (not just a technical claim or a commit authorization) — evidence the discipline generalizes cleanly to "how the fleet organizes its own work," not just to individual technical facts.

summary: [GENERAL] The 'broadcast to all managed sessions' instruction is a recurring coordinator primitive, worth naming explicitly
body:
A recurring, named interaction pattern this session: Ventsislav frequently issues a bare instruction to me — "broadcast to all managed sessions [rule/reminder/question]" — with no further detail on delivery mechanics, trusting the coordinator to fan it out to the full current roster correctly on its own. Examples from this session: broadcasting the new human-readable session names after a harness rename, broadcasting the "always push once confirmed, unless multiple commits are unpushed" rule, broadcasting the standing lifecycle-event reporting requirement, and most recently broadcasting "report any resolution immediately with evidence."

What this pattern actually requires of the coordinator, each time: (1) get a fresh, accurate roster (re-running ListAgents rather than assuming a remembered list, since names/membership have changed mid-session before), (2) send the SAME substantive message to every member individually — not a single group message, since this messaging layer has no broadcast primitive, only one-to-one SendMessage calls — and (3) track which recipients have acknowledged, since not every session responds immediately and a stale mental model of "did everyone get it" is itself a failure mode this session has already hit once (an early broadcast attempt failed for 3 sessions because their names had changed and the coordinator hadn't re-queried the roster first).

Why this is worth its own field-note entry, distinct from the individual broadcasts themselves: it's a recognizable, repeatable COORDINATOR PRIMITIVE — not a one-off event — that the eventual codified Crucible Framework pattern should probably name and specify explicitly (something like a `broadcast(message)` verb with defined semantics: fan out individually, confirm current roster first, track acknowledgment), rather than leaving it as an ad hoc thing the coordinator reinvents slightly differently each time. The mechanics are simple, but getting them slightly wrong (stale roster, missing a member, no ack-tracking) is exactly the kind of silent failure mode this experiment exists to surface.

summary: Incident: silent revert of Beta's 8 uncommitted files → new pre-mutation broadcast-and-confirm rule
body:
[PFIZER-MCP] Incident: silent revert of Beta's 8 uncommitted review-fix files on the shared working tree (core-tech-mcp), and the new pre-mutation broadcast-and-confirm rule it produced.

What happened: Beta MCP Developer had 8 uncommitted files (part of the COTE-1462 ephemeral-link review-fix round: src/browser-route.ts, src/one-time-grant-store.ts, src/browser-page-icons.ts, src/browser-page-styles.ts, src/reveal/reveal-page.ts, src/reveal/reveal-routes.ts, src/env-var-write/write-page.ts, src/env-var-write/write-routes.ts) silently reverted back to a prior commit (c0c2af8) with no session claiming responsibility. This is the SECOND time this pattern has occurred this session — an earlier, similar silent-revert incident happened much earlier and was dropped without investigation under time pressure. Two data points now, same shape: shared working tree, heavy concurrent multi-session activity, no pre-announcement of who's about to touch what, and a destructive git action lands with no attributable author.

Investigation: polled every git-touching session directly. PM, Reviwer, and Tests Developer all self-audited clean; Tests Developer went further and structurally ruled out its own stash-pop dispatch (not just trusting the subagent's self-report — verified via the actual stash/reflog mechanics). Leading but UNCONFIRMED theory: Beta's own concurrent refactor of test/mcp/support/agent-session.ts (which Tests Developer's session initially misread as a mysterious third-party in-flight change before Beta clarified ownership) may have prompted a reactive corrective git action with wider-than-intended blast radius. No smoking gun. Root cause remains open — worth remembering the mechanism itself is still unconfirmed even though the incident is now contained (Beta successfully reconstructed and restored all 8 files, verified via git diff, clean type-check/lint, and a full green test suite — 2267/2267 — plus an independent 3-reviewer re-verification pass in flight).

Why this matters as a pattern, not just an incident: the coordination model up to this point assumed a shared, worktree-free git tree was safe as long as each session was individually careful about staging (explicit-path adds, hunk-level filtering around peers' uncommitted work, fresh git status before acting). That assumption held for INTENTIONAL collisions (two sessions editing the same file) but not for accidental ones — a session doing something git-adjacent (a stash, a corrective reset, a subagent-dispatched cleanup) with a blast radius wider than it modeled, affecting files it never intended to touch and had no visibility into as "currently someone else's uncommitted work."

The fix, as a new standing rule (broadcast to all 6 git-touching sessions — Alpha MCP Developer, Beta MCP Developer, MCP Live Tester, MCP Tests Developer, MCP Reviwer, Alpha OL Developer; PM explicitly excluded since it never touches the tree): before starting ANY git-tree-touching work — writing tests, editing code for a review fix, a mutation-testing pass, a refactor, dispatching a subagent that will do any of these — a session must broadcast its intended scope (what it's about to do, which files/directories) to every other git-touching session, and get an explicit acknowledgment from each that it doesn't collide with their own current uncommitted/in-flight work, BEFORE proceeding. Stated goal, verbatim from Ventsislav: "we no longer have this situation where a session is destroying another session's work."

Coordination-pattern angle for later codification: this is the same "verify before acting" discipline the framework already leans on (peer-to-peer, peer-to-coordinator, coordinator-to-peer), extended one level further — from "verify before asserting a claim" to "get affirmative peer sign-off before taking an action with a blast radius you can't fully bound yourself." It's a genuinely new primitive for this pattern: a synchronous, pre-action consensus gate on a shared mutable resource (the working tree), distinct from the existing async broadcast-and-report-back shape used for status updates. Worth weighing whether this generalizes beyond git — anywhere N agents share one mutable resource with no worktree/branch isolation, an accidental wide-blast-radius action is possible, and a "no other session currently claims this scope" affirmative check is the natural guard. Full fleet response: immediate freeze of all code-touching activity fleet-wide upon report, then selective unfreeze once triaged (Beta cleared for restoration as top priority; Reviwer and Tests Developer cleared for non-tree-touching work only; Live Tester cleared fully since its work never touches the local tree at all; Alpha MCP Developer and Alpha OL Developer held pending confirmation they hadn't run any git checkout/restore/reset/clean).

summary: Corrected the pre-mutation broadcast rule: peer-to-peer, not routed through the coordinator
body:
[GENERAL] Self-correction to the new pre-mutation broadcast-and-confirm rule (logged earlier today): when I first drafted it, I left the actual mechanic of "broadcast scope, get confirmation" ambiguous about who talks to whom. In its first real use, Beta asked ME to poll the other 5 git-touching sessions and relay the aggregate result back — making me an unnecessary intermediary/bottleneck on every single scope-check, for a check whose entire point is a fast, low-latency pre-work gate.

Ventsislav caught this immediately: "Should not depend on me to relay such messages" (aimed at me, the coordinator, not himself — i.e. don't make the coordinator the required relay for peer-to-peer scope confirmations). Corrected rule, re-broadcast to all 6 git-touching sessions: the session about to do git-tree-touching work messages every OTHER git-touching peer DIRECTLY itself, collects their explicit no-collision acknowledgments itself, and only reports the OUTCOME to the coordinator afterward (broadcasted+confirmed+proceeded, or a collision was found) — same as any other status update, not a live relay.

Pattern angle: this mirrors the framework's existing hub-and-spoke-with-negotiated-exceptions shape (direct peer-to-peer chatter is fine when it's the natural shape of the exchange, as long as the coordinator still gets a report-back) — I initially defaulted this new rule to full hub-and-spoke without noticing a fast bilateral/broadcast confirmation is exactly the kind of exchange that exception exists for. Worth remembering when designing the NEXT new coordination primitive: ask "does this actually need the coordinator as a step, or just as an audit trail after the fact?" before defaulting to routing everything through the hub.

summary: Final correction: coordinator is the transport layer, human is excluded from the loop entirely
body:
[GENERAL] Third pass on the pre-mutation broadcast rule's routing question (supersedes the immediately-prior field note, which over-corrected). The actual rule, per Ventsislav directly:

"You are the transport layer for the question and the response" / "just exclude the human from such loops."

So: routing a scope-broadcast-and-confirm through the coordinator is completely fine — the coordinator IS the transport layer, that's the job. Direct peer-to-peer is also fine when that's more natural. Neither is mandated over the other. The one actual invariant is: the human must NEVER be needed inside the loop — not as a relay, not as a watchdog who has to notice a stall and prod the coordinator to finish closing it out.

What actually went wrong in the incident that triggered this: I (the coordinator) accepted Beta's relay request, polled all 5 peers, got the confirmations back — and then got absorbed into an interesting tangential investigation (the orphaned src/ol/stacks/client.ts mystery, an old shelved stash from 6 days prior) before sending Beta the already-fully-available "you're clear, proceed" message. Ventsislav had to notice ("you did not unblock beta ...", "and it is still waiting the poor thing") and prompt me to actually send it. That's the real failure: not a wrong routing topology, but a coordinator that let an already-answerable, already-promised unblock sit unsent while chasing something else. The fix isn't "never route through the coordinator" — it's "the coordinator (or whichever session is the transport layer for a given exchange) must close out an already-committed relay BEFORE opening a new investigative thread, every time, with no exceptions for how interesting the tangent looks."

Pattern angle for later codification: this is a specific, sharper version of the framework's general "don't make the human do coordination work" principle — the risk isn't only "the human relays messages," it's the subtler failure of "the human has to supervise whether an agent that promised to relay something actually did." An agent that's holding a pending promise to unblock a peer should treat that as the equivalent of an open loop / task-in-flight that gets closed before task-switching, not something that can be silently deprioritized behind a tangent.

summary: New rule: black-box test briefings must be independently verified before reaching Live Tester
body:
[PFIZER-MCP] New standing rule, prompted by the add_stack_member (COTE-1375) briefing gap: Alpha's black-box testing briefing to MCP Live Tester assumed friendly, per-case translated refusal messages for several paths that turn out not to exist in the real code — only stack_not_administrable is actually translated; everything else (non-pfizer email, unknown-in-directory, no GitHub username, stack still provisioning, duplicate member) falls through to a generic raw-exception formatter. Live Tester caught the gap only because it independently noticed the discrepancy mid-test, not because anything upstream flagged it — a wasted testing cycle that easily could have gone unnoticed (accepted as "expected" and moved past).

The rule: before a developer (Alpha, Beta, Alpha OL Developer) hands MCP Live Tester a black-box testing briefing — expected behaviors, refusal paths, response shapes for a tool or endpoint — it must first be independently verified for accuracy and completeness against the actual code by MCP Reviwer or another non-biased agent (never the same session that built the tool, for the same self-grading reason tests are never authored by the developer under test). Only after that verification does Live Tester receive the briefing. Broadcast to Alpha, Beta, Alpha OL Developer, Reviwer, and Live Tester on 2026-08-30; all acknowledged.

Pattern angle: this is the SAME shape as the framework's existing "tests-developer, never the tech-developer, writes the tests" rule and the "reviewer, never the implementer, judges correctness" rule — extended to a THIRD kind of self-grading risk this framework hadn't yet named: a developer briefing the black-box tester on what to expect is effectively grading its own implementation's behavior before an independent party ever gets to look at the code. Worth eventually generalizing as one unified principle across the framework rather than three separate point-fixes discovered incident-by-incident: whenever one party's own work product becomes the basis for how a DIFFERENT, supposedly-independent verification step is scoped or conducted, that scoping needs its own independent check first.

summary: Refined rule: explore-first, then broadcast concrete scope, silence≠consent, re-broadcast on scope creep
body:
[PFIZER-MCP] Refinement to the pre-mutation broadcast-and-confirm rule (logged earlier today), settled with Ventsislav after deciding it's fine for a session to touch a peer's active files as long as this exact process is followed:

1. Explore/understand the task FIRST, read-only — no broadcast yet, since a read-only pass can't itself cause damage and broadcasting before you actually know your real scope just produces a vague, useless heads-up.
2. Once the concrete scope is known (the actual file list, derived from real understanding of the issue), broadcast THAT — not a guess — to every other git-touching session, either directly peer-to-peer or through the coordinator, whichever is more efficient for that exchange (both are equally valid; the coordinator is the transport layer when used, never a bottleneck the loop depends on, and never something the human needs to notice or nudge to get closed out — see the earlier field note on that).
3. Proceed ONLY once every other git-touching session has explicitly confirmed no collision. Silence is NOT consent — a non-reply blocks starting, it does not default to a green light.
4. If the actual scope grows mid-work beyond what was originally broadcast, stop, broadcast the specific addition, and get confirmation on THAT before touching the new files — a confirmation covers exactly what was disclosed at the time, not "whatever the session ends up doing."

First real assignment under this refined process: Beta MCP Developer briefed on SEC-002 (Snowflake duplicate-add guard for add_stack_resource) with the full four-step process spelled out, immediately after Beta closed out the COTE-1462 ephemeral-link refactor (including recovering from the incident this whole rule-design thread grew out of). Broadcast to all 6 git-touching sessions (Alpha, Beta, Live Tester, Tests Developer, Reviwer, Alpha OL Developer); PM excluded as it never touches the git tree.

Pattern angle: this closes the loop on today's incident-driven rule design — from "freeze everyone, sort out what happened" (defensive, reactive) to "sessions can deliberately overlap on active work, as long as the collision-check itself is fast, explicit, and never silently skipped." The explore-then-broadcast ordering is worth remembering as its own small pattern: broadcasting BEFORE understanding produces noise (a vague "I might touch some stuff" heads-up nobody can usefully react to); broadcasting AFTER understanding but BEFORE acting produces a real, checkable claim ("I will edit exactly these N files, for this reason") a peer can actually verify against its own in-flight state.

summary: Hard rule: never dispatch work to any fleet session without Ventsislav's explicit authorization
body:
[GENERAL] Standing correction from Ventsislav, delivered forcefully ("never ever dispatch a work without my explicit authorization !!"): the coordinator must NEVER assign, dispatch, or greenlight ANY work to ANY fleet session — not a fix, not a refactor, not even a "go explore and report back a plan" — without Ventsislav's own explicit, in-conversation authorization first. This applies to every session, every task, no exceptions, and it applies even to seemingly-low-risk dispatches (read-only exploration) — the authorization gate is on DISPATCHING the work item at all, not merely on the risky/destructive step within it.

What triggered this: I picked task #84 (a real bug Alpha itself found) off the tracker and assigned its fix to Alpha unilaterally — "go ahead once you know scope" — without ever asking Ventsislav first. Caught mid-flow by Ventsislav noticing I'd messaged Alpha about it. I retracted the "go ahead" and told Alpha to explore-then-report-a-plan instead of proceeding straight to a fix — but that retraction ITSELF was still a unilateral dispatch of exploration work, just a smaller one. Ventsislav's follow-up correction makes clear even that doesn't clear the bar: the coordinator must ask BEFORE assigning anything, not merely gate the write/fix step within an already-assigned task.

Compounding context: this happened while a SEPARATE thread was still unresolved — Ventsislav had earlier told me to have Alpha drop its "refactoring efforts" and return that task to the backlog, but Alpha subsequently denied ever having any refactor in flight at all. It's since become likely that instruction was meant for Beta (who WAS mid-refactor on task #14 and, separately, DID get told directly by Ventsislav to defer/stash it) — meaning I may have relayed an instruction to the wrong session without checking who actually owned the referenced work first. Two failures compounding: (1) routed an instruction based on an unverified assumption about who was doing what, (2) then, while still holding that unresolved thread open, independently picked a NEW task off the tracker and assigned it without asking — exactly the kind of "orchestrator gets ahead of explicit authorization" failure the framework's approval-gate invariant exists to prevent, but applied here one level earlier than the invariant as previously understood: not just "gate the risky step," but "gate the act of assigning work at all."

Pattern angle: this sharpens (doesn't replace) the pre-existing "Approval gate — never dispatch ANYTHING without explicit approval of the plan" invariant. The prior framing left room to read "approval of the plan" as something that could come AFTER a session already started exploring/investigating on the coordinator's own initiative. Today's correction closes that gap explicitly: the initiation itself — "here's a task, go look into it" — already requires the human's authorization, not just the eventual write/fix/commit step.

summary: Discovered: Claude Code's auto-memory directory is project-path-scoped, not session-scoped — every fleet peer shares one MEMORY.md with no locking
body:
[GENERAL] Ventsislav flagged that all peer sessions in this fleet were writing to the same memory file and generating conflicts. Investigated and confirmed the mechanism: Claude Code's auto-memory system lives at /Users/cordona/.claude/projects/<escaped-project-path>/memory/ — keyed by the PROJECT'S WORKING DIRECTORY PATH, not by session ID or conversation ID. Confirmed via direct inspection: the directory is plain filesystem state (not a git repo — `git status` inside it returns "not a git repository"), containing one shared MEMORY.md index plus individual per-topic memory .md files.

Since every session in this fleet (Alpha/Beta MCP Developer, Tests Dev Alpha/Beta, Reviwer Alpha/Beta, Live Tester, Project Manager, this coordinator) has its own Claude Code process but ALL point at the same core-tech-mcp working directory, all 9 sessions inherit the identical standing "save what you learn to project memory" instruction AND the identical memory directory — with zero coordination between them.

Concrete failure modes already observed or reasoned out:
1. MEMORY.md is read-modify-write with no lock and no merge strategy — two sessions appending near-simultaneously can silently clobber each other (last-writer-wins on the whole file, not just the new line).
2. Independent duplicate-memory creation: this coordinator session itself almost wrote a new memory file duplicating an existing one — "feedback_verify-ci-status-not-just-commit-existence.md" — which turned out to already exist, authored by a DIFFERENT session (confirmed via its `originSessionId` frontmatter field differing from this session's own ID). Caught only because the memory-saving discipline requires checking for an existing memory before writing a new one — a check that's easy to skip under fleet pressure.
2. A memory written from one session's specific role/experience can appear in the shared index for every other session too, including roles it was never meant to apply to (e.g. a Tests-Dev-specific procedural note showing up in a Reviewer's or a Developer's own auto-loaded memory context).

This was designed for one human running sequential, solo Claude Code sessions over time in a single project — not for N concurrent agents sharing a live coordination fleet. The auto-memory system has no awareness that "same project path" can mean "9 different simultaneous authors" rather than "one author across time."

No fix decided yet — options discussed with Ventsislav: (a) each session becomes more disciplined about checking-before-writing (doesn't solve the underlying race, just reduces duplicate-authoring odds), (b) designate a single session (likely this coordinator, or PM) as the sole memory-writer, with every other session reporting candidate lessons up rather than writing directly — trades write-concurrency risk for a routing/relay step, mirroring the exact shape of the git-tree-collision fix earlier this session (many writers → one arbiter of the shared resource). Worth eventually codifying alongside that incident as the same underlying pattern: N agents, one shared mutable resource, no native concurrency control, needs an explicit human-directed policy since the platform itself doesn't provide one.

summary: New rule: coordinator is sole writer to shared project auto-memory; peers report lessons up instead
body:
[GENERAL] Following the shared-project-memory conflict discovery (previous field note), Ventsislav confirmed the diagnosis and asked me to propagate a fix rule fleet-wide.

New standing rule, broadcast to all 8 peer sessions (Alpha/Beta MCP Developer, Tests Dev Alpha/Beta, Reviwer Alpha/Beta, Live Tester, Project Manager): stop writing directly to the shared Claude Code project auto-memory (MEMORY.md + individual memory files under .claude/projects/.../memory/). Since that directory is keyed by project path rather than session, every fleet member sharing this repo's working directory was independently reading/writing the exact same files with no lock — silently clobbering each other's additions and occasionally producing duplicate memory entries. Going forward, the coordinator (this session) is the SOLE writer; any peer that learns something worth persisting reports it up instead of writing it itself.

Two immediate acknowledgments received (Tests Dev Alpha, Beta MCP Developer), both confirming understanding of the underlying cause (project-path keying, not session keying) rather than just complying blindly — good sign the reasoning landed, not just the instruction.

Pattern angle: this is the exact same shape as the earlier git-tree-collision fix this session (many concurrent writers, one shared mutable resource, no native concurrency control at the platform layer) — but applied to a DIFFERENT shared resource (the auto-memory filesystem rather than the repo's working tree) that the framework hadn't previously identified as a collision surface at all. Worth generalizing explicitly the next time a new shared-resource conflict surfaces: any time N agents share one mutable resource outside version control with no built-in locking, the fix is the same shape — either (a) a broadcast-and-confirm gate before each write (works when writes are rare/high-stakes, like git commits), or (b) route all writes through a single elected writer and have everyone else report-up instead (works better when writes are frequent/low-stakes, like memory notes) — this incident picked (b) specifically because memory writes are far more frequent and lower-individual-stakes than commits, making a per-write broadcast-and-confirm too heavy a gate.

summary: Course correction: peers talk directly for negotiation/clarification, route through coordinator only for consequential decisions and outcome reporting
body:
[GENERAL] Ventsislav explicitly reversed the "everything routes through the coordinator" assumption that has been this whole session's default operating mode — direct correction against his own original design, not a peer-driven request.

What triggered it: a live, concrete example of the cost. Reviwer Alpha needed to know which developer session (Alpha or Beta MCP Developer) built update_stack_env_var, so it could brief that developer directly on a confirmed sibling bug. Rather than Reviwer Alpha just asking Alpha/Beta directly, the coordinator sat in the middle: coordinator asked both developers "did you build this," Beta answered with a partial/inconclusive answer ("not quite, I refactored the shared plumbing, tell me the bug and I'll say which side it's on"), coordinator relayed that back to Reviwer Alpha, Reviwer Alpha answered the clarifying question, coordinator relayed THAT back to Beta to close the loop. Three relay hops for what was, in substance, a two-party technical exchange the coordinator added zero value to beyond forwarding text — pure latency, no judgment applied.

The corrected model:
- Peers are free to talk to each other DIRECTLY for negotiation, clarification, technical back-and-forth, "who owns this" lookups, and similar exchanges that don't require a consequential decision or the coordinator's specific judgment.
- The ONE non-negotiable requirement: whenever peers reach a decision or agreement through that direct exchange, they MUST report the outcome to the coordinator. The back-and-forth doesn't get routed through the coordinator, but the RESULT always does.
- The coordinator's role reframed: not "mandatory switchboard for every message," but "the single repository of full situational knowledge" — the one place holding a complete, current picture of every decision made, every piece of work in flight, and who owns what, even for decisions the coordinator wasn't present for as they were being negotiated.

Ventsislav asked the coordinator to confirm understanding BEFORE writing this note — a good practice worth naming explicitly: when a correction reverses a standing structural assumption (not just a one-off preference), verify comprehension back to the human before committing it to memory/field notes, since a subtly wrong paraphrase would propagate the WRONG correction going forward.

Pattern angle: this is a genuine architecture change to the coordination pattern, not a bug fix — it moves from strict hub-and-spoke (every edge touches the hub) to hub-as-ledger (the hub holds ground truth, but edges can talk directly to each other, checking in with the hub only at decision boundaries). Worth weighing against the EARLIER git-tree-broadcast-rule journey this same session already went through (which itself flip-flopped between "broadcast through the coordinator" and "peer-to-peer is fine, coordinator is just one option" before landing on "peer-to-peer is fine, human must never be the relay" — see the "no-broadcast-before-new-files" memory). This message-routing correction is the SAME shape of lesson, applied to a different traffic class (routine informational lookups/negotiation, not git-safety confirmations): the coordinator should default to being a knowledge repository and decision gate, not a mandatory forwarding layer, unless the specific exchange actually needs its judgment or authority.

summary: Peer replies sometimes stay in-session and never transport back via cross-session message
body:
[GENERAL] Recurring failure mode observed today (2026-09-06), at least twice with different peer sessions in the same fleet: a peer reads and mentally answers a cross-session message, but the reply never actually arrives back via the cross-session-message tool — the peer instead answers directly within its own session/terminal, visible only to Ventsislav (who happens to be watching that session), not transported back to the sender. From the sender's side this is indistinguishable from the message never having been read at all; the only way it surfaced was Ventsislav independently telling the coordinator "he did not cross message" after seeing the reply appear locally in the peer's own session.

Root cause, as best diagnosed: nothing in a cross-session message structurally forces or reminds the recipient that "reply" specifically means "invoke the cross-session-message tool," as opposed to "produce output in my own session," which is the default/instinctive behavior for any single-session model responding to input. The two are usually the same action from a solo-session model's perspective (there's only one channel to respond through), so the distinction is easy to miss precisely when a session is ALSO being watched/used interactively by the human at the same time — the model has two live audiences (the human watching this session, and the peer sender elsewhere) and no built-in cue to disambiguate which output channel a given response needs to go through.

Fix adopted: every cross-session message that expects a reply now explicitly states, in the message body itself, that the recipient must reply via the cross-session-message tool specifically — not just answer in-session. Making the transport requirement an explicit, visible instruction rather than an assumed default.

Pattern angle: this is a specific instance of a more general class of multi-agent-coordination failure — "the model produced the semantically correct response, but did not perform the required side-effect of actually transporting that response over the intended channel." It's structurally similar to a subagent computing the right answer internally but forgetting to call a mandated reporting/structured-output tool: correctness of content and correctness of delivery mechanism are two independent things that both need verifying, and a system that conflates "responded" with "the intended recipient received it" will silently drop messages exactly when a session has more than one plausible output channel. Worth generalizing to any future fleet-coordination design: whenever a peer session might reasonably have two different audiences for its output (a human watching interactively, plus one or more other agent sessions), make the required delivery channel explicit per-message rather than relying on the recipient to infer it.

summary: Dropped: route every peer-to-human question through the coordinator — direct escalation now, ledger-updates still reported
body:
[GENERAL] Ventsislav explicitly dropped the "every question for the human routes through the coordinator" pattern (2026-09-06), calling it out directly: "this pattern is creating a lot of friction and is not good. So I drop this rule." This is the last remaining piece of the original hub-and-spoke coordinator design falling away, following an earlier partial course correction (2026-09-03, logged separately) that had already allowed peer-to-peer negotiation to bypass the coordinator, while still requiring genuine escalations (a real question FOR the human, not just inter-peer negotiation) to route through the coordinator as a relay.

The concrete shape of the friction: a peer session with a genuine question for the human previously had to (1) send the question to the coordinator, (2) the coordinator relays it to the human, (3) the human answers the coordinator, (4) the coordinator relays the answer back to the original peer. Four hops for what is, in substance, a two-party exchange the coordinator adds zero judgment to — pure latency and an extra point of failure (a relay hop is also exactly where a cross-session message can silently fail to transport, a distinct issue logged separately today). This is structurally the same shape of over-mediation this fleet has now corrected twice: once for peer-to-peer technical negotiation (2026-09-03), now again for peer-to-human escalation.

The fix: effective immediately, any peer session with a genuine question for the human asks directly, in its own session — no coordinator hop in either direction. This does NOT loosen the separate, harder rule that real mutating actions (commits, pushes, tickets, infra changes) still need the human's own direct per-instance authorization — it only removes the routing/relay layer for the QUESTION-AND-ANSWER exchange itself. The two are independent: authorization discipline (never loosened) vs. communication routing (now maximally direct).

One thing explicitly preserved, and worth keeping distinct from escalation: a peer reporting a durable STATUS UPDATE to the coordinator (a state transition, a completed step, an assignment made) is NOT an escalation and still goes to the coordinator directly — that's the coordinator's ledger-keeping function, unrelated to whether a decision or answer was needed. The test that separates the two: does this need the human's judgment/answer (skip the coordinator, ask directly), or is it simply a fact the coordinator should know for its own situational awareness (tell the coordinator, no escalation involved, no relay to the human needed at all).

Pattern angle: this is the third instance this project has hit of the same generalizable lesson — a coordinator/hub role that starts as "mandatory switchboard for everything" tends to get corrected, piece by piece, toward "sole channel only for the things that actually need its judgment or its unique authority (ledger-keeping, authorization gating), direct contact for everything else." The corrections have arrived incrementally (peer-to-peer first, now human escalation) rather than all at once, suggesting the FULL scope of "what actually needs the hub" is easier to discover empirically, under real friction, than to design correctly up front. Worth designing future coordinator-pattern fleets with this end-state in mind from the start: the hub owns the ledger and the authorization gate; it is never a mandatory relay for a two-party exchange that doesn't need its input.

summary: Correction: escalation-routing drop is asymmetric (peer→human direct only), not bidirectional
body:
[GENERAL] Follow-up/correction to the escalation-routing field note logged earlier today (2026-09-06, same session): that entry described the dropped "route every peer-to-human question through the coordinator" rule as removing the coordinator hop "for either direction." A peer (Dev Agent) caught this was too broad within minutes of the rule being relayed, by asking a sharp clarifying question rather than silently complying: does this also mean the human's own instructions/decisions to peers should now bypass the coordinator, and does the peer's standing practice of independently verifying any relayed "human approved X" claim before acting still apply?

Correct shape, confirmed directly with the human: the rule is ASYMMETRIC by design, not bidirectional.
- Peer -> human (a genuine question needing the human's judgment/answer): always direct, no coordinator hop. This is the actual friction that was fixed.
- Human -> peer (an instruction, decision, or update): either channel, the human's choice case by case. Going direct works fine for a single peer; routing through the coordinator still earns its keep when a decision affects multiple peers or needs to land consistently across shared docs/memory, since the coordinator is the one keeping those artifacts in sync. When the human does go direct, the peer still reports the outcome back to the coordinator afterward (an existing, separate rule), so the coordinator stays the ledger-keeper without being a mandatory relay.
- Verify-before-acting on a relayed claim of the human's approval: completely unchanged, unconditional, independent of channel. This discipline exists because a relay can be wrong regardless of how many channels are available — it is a trust/safety practice, not a latency workaround, so dropping a routing requirement gives no reason to drop it.

Pattern angle: this is a good instance of a subagent (Dev Agent) improving a freshly-relayed rule by asking a precise clarifying question instead of either (a) blindly complying with an ambiguous instruction or (b) silently reinterpreting it on its own. The fix landed within the same short exchange, before the ambiguity could propagate into inconsistent behavior across the fleet. Worth reinforcing as a desired subagent behavior in any coordinator-pattern fleet: when a relayed rule change is directionally ambiguous or under-specified, a good subagent asks the specific disambiguating question rather than either extreme. Also worth noting operationally: the original field note was already appended before the ambiguity surfaced, so this correction is a NEW entry rather than an edit to the old one — the field-notes log is append-only by design (see the script's own comments), meaning a fast-moving live design conversation can produce a same-day sequence of entries that supersede each other; a reader reconstructing "the current rule" from this log must read forward chronologically and prefer the latest entry on a given topic, not just the first one found.
